items.value: Good and bad have no meaning in the natural state; the categories of right and wrong come into existence only with the civil state
items.reasoning: The passage says plainly that nothing in a natural state can be called good or bad by common assent, and that sin 'cannot be conceived in a natural state, but only in a civil state, which is decreed by common consent what is good or bad'. That is exactly option A: the conceptions of right and wrong exist because a state has been formed. B is wrong because the passage attributes the decision to 'common consent', not to a ruling authority, and it never claims men would fail to be morally right. C is contradicted by the passage: if nothing in the natural state can be called good or bad, a man there cannot be 'immoral' at all, only self-interested. D introduces survival of the species, which the passage never raises.

items.value: Statements 2, 3 and 5 only follow; 1 (too much globalization) and 4 (own supply chains) are unsupported
items.reasoning: Statement 2 follows: a car driving in Dublin, coded in California and maintained from Hyderabad, with transnational insurance and investment consequences, is technology blurring economic borders. Statement 3 follows: the passage asks whether the Irish Government, the original code writer or an outsourced programmer decides how a car values a human life, which places a private innovator inside a domain that belonged to the State. Statement 5 follows from 'This will pose conundrums' and from different national jurisdictions carrying different fine print, which is exactly ambiguity that geopolitics must absorb. Statement 1 is not supported anywhere in the passage, which never argues that globalization has gone too far, and Statement 4 is not either, since supply chains are never mentioned. C is the only option that excludes both 1 and 4.

items.value: Systemic or structural reform of the banking system, not bad-debt resolution or recapitalisation, is the long-term answer to bad loans
items.reasoning: The passage concedes that the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and recapitalisation help, then turns on them: they 'are only a part of the solution' and can do little to rein in reckless lending, and it closes with 'Unless there are systemic reforms that address the problem of unsustainable lending, future credit cycles will continue to stress the banking system.' Option D restates that suggestion. A is not implied, since the passage asks for systemic reform rather than Central Government monitoring. B is contradicted in spirit: cheap credit that induces more lending is closer to the reckless lending the passage warns about. C names bank mergers, which the passage never mentions.

items.value: Because monetary policy cannot work without the active support of fiscal policy, the central bank cannot operate independently of the Government
items.reasoning: The passage's only substantive claim is that neither wing of macroeconomic policy, monetary or fiscal, can work independently without the active support of the other. Monetary policy is conducted by the central bank and fiscal policy by the Government, so the direct corollary is option A. B, C and D each import something the passage never says: close regulation of financial markets, an incompatibility between market economy and socialist policy, and financial sector reforms respectively. Runner-up is D, which borrows the passage's phrase about enhancing economic welfare; D would win only if the examiner read A as a claim about central bank institutional independence, a doctrine the passage does not discuss, rather than as a statement about policy coordination. Even then D has to supply 'reforms', a word absent from the passage, which is why A is preferred.

items.value: B is the fastest scorer over the match: 55 runs off 97 balls, a strike rate of 56.70 against A 42.86, C 28.00 and D 23.81
items.reasoning: Speed of scoring is runs per ball, and a Test Match means both innings taken together. Combining the two innings gives A 75 runs off 175 balls (42.86), B 55 off 97 (56.70), C 35 off 125 (28.00) and D 25 off 105 (23.81), so B is the fastest. Note that A has the single fastest individual innings, 61 off 99 at 61.62 in the first innings, but A then took 76 balls for 14 in the second, which drags the match figure well below B's. Reading the table innings by innings would leave the question undefined, since it asks about the Test Match as a whole, which is why the four columns are meant to be aggregated.

items.value: At least 2/15 of the villagers are both literate and under 25, so some villagers under 25 are certainly literate
items.reasoning: One-third of the villagers are literate and four-fifths are under 25, so only one-fifth are 25 or over. If no under-25 villager were literate, every literate person would have to fit inside that one-fifth, but the literates are one-third, which is larger. So at least 1/3 minus 1/5, that is 2/15 of the villagers, are both literate and under 25, making B certainly correct. A is certainly false, because half own houses while only a third are literate, so the house-owners cannot all be literate. D is certainly false by the same counting: at least 1/2 minus 1/5, that is 3/10, are under 25 and own a house. C is simply undetermined, as nothing links paddy cultivation to literacy.

items.value: Statement-2 alone fixes the 14th as a Wednesday; Statement-1 alone leaves four possible answers because the month length is unknown
items.reasoning: Statement-2 says the third Saturday was the 17th, so the 17th is a Saturday and counting back three days makes the 14th a Wednesday. That is sufficient on its own. Statement-1 says only that the last day is a Wednesday, and the month length is not given: a 28-day month makes the 14th a Wednesday, a 29-day month a Tuesday, a 30-day month a Monday and a 31-day month a Sunday. Since it yields four different answers, Statement-1 alone is insufficient, so the correct choice is B rather than C, which would require both statements.

items.value: 10 October 2027 falls on a Sunday
items.reasoning: Working from 1 January 2000, a Saturday, the 27 years to 1 January 2027 contain 7 leap days (2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024), giving 27 times 365 plus 7 equals 9862 days; 9862 leaves remainder 6 on division by 7, so 1 January 2027 is a Friday. 2027 is not a leap year, so 10 October is day 283 of the year, which is 282 days after 1 January; 282 leaves remainder 2 on division by 7, so the day is Friday plus 2, a Sunday. As a cross-check, 1 October 2027 is exactly 273 days after 1 January and 273 is divisible by 7, so 1 October is also a Friday, making the 8th a Friday and the 10th a Sunday.

items.value: None of the four conclusions follows; two particular premises sharing a middle term yield no definite conclusion
items.reasoning: Both premises are particular: some greens are blues, and some blues are blacks. The greens that are blues need not be any of the blues that are blacks, so nothing definite links greens to blacks. Conclusion-1 (some greens are blacks) is possible but not necessary, and Conclusion-2 (no green is black) is likewise possible but not necessary; they are contradictories, so option A, which asserts that both follow, is impossible. Conclusion-3 (all greens are blacks) and Conclusion-4 (all blacks are greens) are universals that the particular premises cannot support, which rules out B and C. Hence D. Note that in the standard complementary-pair convention one would say 'either 1 or 2 follows', but that is not offered among the options, and neither follows on its own.

items.value: X = 607; each term is three times the previous term plus one
items.reasoning: The rule is multiply by 3 and add 1: 2 gives 7, 7 gives 22, 22 gives 67, and 67 gives 202. Applying it once more, 202 times 3 plus 1 is 607, and the rule is confirmed by the next term, since 607 times 3 plus 1 is 1822, exactly the value printed at the end of the sequence. The nearby options 603, 605 and 608 all fail that check, because only 607 reproduces 1822.

items.value: Top-quality higher education can be delivered more widely and at lower cost, through free video lectures and the flipped classroom, without any loss of content quality
items.reasoning: The passage's two movements are that the best universities are shifting to the flipped classroom, and that they have made their video lectures free to anyone in the world while encouraging other institutions to build their own packages around them. Since the lectures come from 'truly excellent teachers', the content is not thinned, and since they are free and reusable worldwide, access becomes easier and cheaper, which is option B. A is wrong because the flipped classroom is a hybrid and the passage never claims online teaching is more effective than conventional teaching. C overreaches into infrastructure spending and social capital, neither of which the passage discusses, and the model still needs classrooms and professors. D shifts to private institutes and coaching, which the passage never mentions.

items.value: Cities must adopt sustainability-related interventions, covering air quality, transport and citizen participation, to be maintained and developed
items.reasoning: The passage sets out the problem, that cities are vulnerable to climate change through population concentration and poor infrastructure and lack systems to respond, and then turns prescriptive: it is important to address air quality and transport as 'vital to identifying sustainable solutions', and citizens must be involved in city planning to create an ecosystem meeting people's needs. Option C is that prescription. B restates a premise and misplaces the blame, since the passage attributes the gap to systems not yet developed rather than to density itself. A introduces municipal autonomy and D introduces public-private partnership, neither of which appears in the passage.

items.value: A pen costs exactly twice a pencil (3p + 5q = 2p + 7q gives p = 2q)
items.reasoning: Let a pen cost p and a pencil q. Jay spent 3p + 5q and Vijay spent 2p + 7q, and the two amounts are equal, so 3p + 5q = 2p + 7q. Cancelling gives p = 2q, that is, a pen costs twice a pencil, which is option C. This also disposes of the others: A is false because the pen is dearer, B is false because the prices are unequal, and D would require p = 3q, which does not satisfy the equation.

items.value: Q scored 360 (P scored 400)
items.reasoning: Let P's score be p. Q scored 40 marks fewer, so Q equals p minus 40, and Q also scored 10 per cent less than P, so Q equals 0.9p. Setting them equal, 0.9p = p minus 40, so 0.1p = 40 and p = 400. Q therefore scored 400 minus 40, which is 360. Checking, 10 per cent of 400 is 40 and 400 minus 40 is 360, so both conditions hold; 400 is P's score, not Q's, which is what makes option C the natural trap.

items.value: X has 80, Y has 120 and Z has 160, so the total is 360 rupees
items.reasoning: Read as printed, the first condition says that after Y hands X 40 rupees, Y is left with half of what Z has, so Y minus 40 equals Z divided by 2; the second says that after Z hands X 40 rupees all three are equal, so X plus 40 equals Y equals Z minus 40. Substituting Z equals Y plus 40 into the first gives 2Y minus 80 equals Y plus 40, so Y is 120, Z is 160 and X is 80, a total of 360. Both conditions check out: Y left with 80 is half of Z's 160, and after Z pays X the three hold 120 each. The stem is garbled, printing 'half of as much as Z' where 'half as much as Z' is meant, so it is flagged rather than repaired; the reading taken above is the only one that lands on a listed option, since reading it as X ending with half of Z gives a total of 120 and reading it as Y ending with half of X gives 240, neither of which is offered. That convergence is what makes B secure despite the defect, and the runner-up would be any option reachable under a different reading, of which there is none.

items.value: CHEMISTRY becomes BIDNHTSSX, letters in odd positions moving back one and letters in even positions moving forward one
items.reasoning: Compare MATHEMATICS with LBSIDNZUHDR position by position: M becomes L and T becomes S and E becomes D, each a step back, while A becomes B and H becomes I and M becomes N, each a step forward; A in the seventh place becomes Z, confirming the backward step wraps around the alphabet. So odd positions shift back one and even positions shift forward one, and applying that rule to MATHEMATICS reproduces LBSIDNZUHDR exactly. Applying it to CHEMISTRY gives C to B, H to I, E to D, M to N, I to H, S to T, T to S, R to S and Y to X, that is BIDNHTSSX, which is option B. Option C is the same string except for L in the fourth place, which would require M to move backward in an even position, contrary to the rule.

items.value: The hands are 180 degrees apart at 60/11 minutes past 7, about 7:05:27, which falls between 7:05 and 7:10
items.reasoning: At t minutes past 7 the hour hand is at 210 plus 0.5t degrees and the minute hand at 6t degrees, so the separation is 210 minus 5.5t. Setting that equal to 180 gives 5.5t = 30, so t = 60/11, about 5.45 minutes, that is roughly 7:05:27. Checking the boundaries confirms it: at 7:00 the separation is 210 degrees, at 7:05 it is 182.5 degrees and at 7:10 it is 155 degrees, so the hands pass through 180 degrees strictly after 7:05 and well before 7:10. Hence option D, not C, since at exactly 7:05 the angle is still 182.5 degrees.

items.value: 9 incorrect responses (81 correct)
items.reasoning: Let c be the number correct and w the number wrong, with c + w = 90 since all questions were attempted. The score gives 5c minus 2w = 387, and substituting w = 90 minus c gives 5c minus 180 plus 2c = 387, so 7c = 567 and c = 81, leaving w = 9. Verifying, 81 correct answers earn 405 marks and 9 wrong answers lose 18, and 405 minus 18 is exactly 387.

items.value: The two possible sums are 142 and 262, whose arithmetic mean is 202
items.reasoning: Reading 3P, 4P and PP as two-digit numerals, the sum is (30 + P) + (40 + P) + 11P + 11P, which equals 70 + 24P. For the total to end in 2 the units digit of 4P must be 2, which happens only for P = 3 and P = 8. P = 3 gives 142, so R = 1 and Q = 4, and P = 8 gives 262, so R = 2 and Q = 6; in both cases P, Q and R are three different digits, as required, and both totals are three-digit numbers of the form RQ2. The mean of 142 and 262 is 404 divided by 2, which is 202. Note that R = 2 in the second case is permitted, because the condition constrains only P, Q and R against each other, not against the fixed units digit 2; excluding it would leave a single sum of 142, which is not among the options.

items.value: P = 8, Q = 5, R = 2, since 85 times 3 is 255, so (P + R) divided by Q is 10 divided by 5, which is 2
items.reasoning: Writing the numbers out, (10P + Q) times 3 equals 100R + 11Q, which simplifies to 30P = 100R + 8Q, or 15P = 50R + 4Q. Since 15P is at most 135, R can only be 1 or 2. For R = 1 the right side runs from 50 to 86 and never hits a multiple of 15, so there is no solution. For R = 2 the right side is 100 + 4Q, and only P = 8 works, giving 120 = 100 + 4Q and so Q = 5. That yields 85 times 3 equals 255, with P, Q and R equal to 8, 5 and 2, all different and R non-zero. Therefore (P + R) divided by Q is 10 divided by 5, which is 2, so the answer is determined and option D is wrong.
